newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Mbeki wants greater role for OAU.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mbeki wants greater role for OAU.

text.p: South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki said in remarks published on Sunday that the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) should have greater powers to intervene in the continent's trouble spots.

"Nobody should be able to hide behind the issue of national sovereignty," Mbeki, who has all but taken over the reins of power from President Nelson Mandela, said in an interview with the Sunday Argus.

Mbeki, who in recent months has been promoting the idea of an African "renaissance", said events in the former Zaire had shown that instability in one country could have repercussions across the continent.
"We cannot say, if something goes wrong in one part of the continent, that because of the doctrine of national sovereignty it is a domestic affair," Mbeki said.
"The OAU should be able to say 'we are concerned'... It requires the development of a continental consensus."

Mbeki, who played a key role in negotiations on Zaire's tumultuous transition into the Democratic Republic of the Congo, said President Laurent Kabila needed to create a climate for democratic activity.
"While preparations are being made for the drawing up of the constitution and for elections, nevertheless democratic processes must be entrenched...
"We hope that some time this week we can take our proposals to them, or that they may come to us," he said.
A U.N. investigator has pointed to 134 separate massacres of Rwandan refugees by forces allied to Kabila in the civil war which brought him to power in May.

Roberto Garreton of Chile suggested the perpetrators should appear before an international war crimes tribunal and said killings and other grave human rights violations had not stopped after Kabila ousted Mobutu Sese Seko.
Kabila's government has rejected the accusations.
Mbeki said the only way to achieve South Africa's dream of a nonracial society was to narrow the gap between poor blacks and those who had attained wealth and status because of apartheid.

"It is important that those sections of our population who sit in privileged positions because of our history realise that their own continued success depends on addressing the challenge of the disadvantaged," he said.
Mbeki said the issue would be high on the agenda at a national conference of the ruling African National Congress in December.
"The conference must discuss what progress has been made in creating this nonracial society...Indeed, what did we mean by a nonracial society?"
